Even Before OpenAI Arrest, Silicon Valley Was Bracing for Spies
 
Plus, suspicions mount over restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink access, and UBS prepares for a once unimaginable move
 
 
RACHEL MENDELSON/WSJ; ISTOCK
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

At a San Francisco playground, a stranger tried to befriend an OpenAI employee who was there with their child. The stranger, also accompanied by a child, made small talk and asked about their work. It was no idle curiosity: The stranger was a spy.

 

OpenAI presented that scenario to its employees to warn them against attempts to steal corporate secrets. The companies racing to build artificial superintelligence say it could reshape entire economies, create vast fortunes and dominate future warfare. The stakes have made the industry a prime espionage target. And while Silicon Valley has been on guard, there’s no such thing as a perfect defense.

 

On Tuesday, Saudi OpenAI employee Abdulrahman Alfozan was charged with planting a recording device behind a conference room TV. Security experts say the threat goes well beyond one hidden device. We examine how AI labs are training employees to spot spies.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Sudden restrictions on Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink terminals sparked panic in Kyiv and unconfirmed suspicions that President Trump ordered Elon Musk to throttle access, underscoring how sharply U.S.-Ukraine relations have soured.

• The Trump administration’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar is aimed at building a case to strip her of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the probe.

 

• Executives at UBS, Switzerland’s last remaining flagship global bank, are preparing for a once unimaginable move—ditching its Swiss home base.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

He crafted a crypto law for Trump—as his company got millions from a crypto giant.

 

While Bo Hines led the White House push for landmark stablecoin legislation, Tether—the world’s largest stablecoin issuer, with the most at stake in the law—was steering millions of dollars to a business he co-owned, according to messages, internal documents and payment records reviewed by the Journal. The Genius Act was signed into law on July 18, 2025, with Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino seated beside Hines at the White House signing ceremony. Three weeks later, Hines announced he was leaving the White House. The following month, Tether named him CEO of its new U.S. division, reports Sam Kessler.

 

5.

 

Meet the far-left firebrand who wants to upend France’s politics and cancel its debt.

 

Jean-Luc Mélenchon has vowed to cancel hundreds of billions of euros in France’s national debt, prosecute its central bank governor, nationalize swaths of the economy and pull out of NATO. And as student protests have washed across the country—blockading hundreds of schools and, in some cases, setting them on fire—the 75-year-old Mélenchon has joined the marches or cheered from the sidelines. Now Mélenchon is emerging as the main rival of Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader and front-runner in next year’s presidential elections. While his rhetoric is energizing part of the French electorate, Mélenchon’s confrontational style and radical economic proposals have spooked much of the country, reports Noemie Bisserbe.

His mother got a new hip. So they went to remote Iceland to road test it.

 

Two years after watching his mother hobble with a cane through crowded Dubrovnik, Croatia, Jamie Lafferty was on a far more rugged trip with her. The difference: She had a new hip. Months after her hip-replacement surgery, the pair set out for Iceland’s little-visited Westfjords—putting both travelers to the test against winding roads, thundering waterfalls and uneven hiking trails.
